passages.happening:
Paul turns to the founding father of Israel. “What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather, has discovered?” (verse 1). If Abraham was justified by what he did, he would have something to boast about, “but not before God” (verse 2).

“For what does the Scripture say?” (verse 3). It says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (verse 3).

He explains with a picture from work. A worker's wages are not a gift; they are owed (verse 4). “However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked, his faith is credited as righteousness” (verse 5).

David says the same, Paul goes on, when he speaks of the happiness of the person to whom God credits righteousness apart from works (verse 6): “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered” (verse 7). “Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Abraham was the great hero of the Jewish people. Every Jewish believer in Rome called him ‘our father’. Any argument about how a person is right with God had to deal with him.

Many Jewish teachers of the time pictured Abraham as the model of faithful obedience. The book of Sirach, written in the second century BC, praises him as one who kept the law of the Most High and was found faithful when he was tested. First Maccabees asks whether Abraham was not found faithful when tested, and it was counted to him as righteousness. That ‘test’ was the offering of Isaac in Genesis 22. Paul reads Genesis differently. He goes back to chapter 15, where Abraham simply trusted God's promise.

‘Credited’ is a word from bookkeeping, logizomai, used of entering a sum in an account. It appears again and again in this chapter. Paul's point is that righteousness was put to Abraham's account, not earned.

Verse 5 would have startled a Jewish hearer. ‘Him who justifies the wicked’. The law told judges never to do that. Paul says God does it, and Paul will explain how he can do it justly: the answer was given in 3:25-26.

Paul links Genesis and the Psalm through one shared word, ‘credit’ or ‘count’, a way of reading Scripture that Jewish teachers used. Abraham was credited with righteousness; David's forgiven man has his sin not counted against him. Put together, being counted righteous includes being forgiven.
passages.ot:
The key verse is Genesis 15:6. Abram was old and had no child. God took him outside and told him to count the stars: “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). Then “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). The site's note on Genesis 15:1-6 explains the verse in its own place and how Paul and James both use it.

The second quotation is Psalm 32, a psalm of David: “Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1), and “Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him” (Psalm 32:2). Paul follows the Greek wording.

The law forbade a judge to acquit the guilty: “I will not acquit the guilty” (Exodus 23:7). Proverbs calls “Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous” detestable to the LORD (Proverbs 17:15). That is why ‘Him who justifies the wicked’ is such a bold phrase.
passages.hard:
How does Romans 4 fit with James 2, which says Abraham was “justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar” (James 2:21)? Both quote Genesis 15:6.

Most readers, across the churches, say they are answering different questions. Paul asks how a sinner is first set right with God, and he means by ‘works’ doing the law as the ground of acceptance. James fights a faith that says it believes but never acts, and he uses ‘justified’ of faith shown to be real. James's example comes from Genesis 22, many years after Genesis 15. Paul himself says what counts is “faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6).

Protestant and Catholic teaching still differ on how faith and works relate in being justified, as the note on Genesis 15:1-6 and the book page set out. These notes do not settle it. All read Paul and James as friends, not enemies.
passages.asks: Paul says God justifies ‘the wicked’ who trust him. Ask whether you believe that includes you, or whether you are still trying to earn wages from God. Then read Psalm 32 slowly. David knew the weight of hidden sin and the joy of forgiveness. Ask what you are still hiding.

passages.t: Before circumcision: the father of all who believe
passages.happening:
Is this blessing only for the circumcised, Paul asks, or for the uncircumcised too (verse 9)? We have been saying that Abraham's faith was credited to him as righteousness.

“In what context was it credited? Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before” (verse 10).

Abraham received circumcision “as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised” (verse 11). So he is the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness might be credited to them too (verse 11).

“And he is also the father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is a simple point about order, and it changes everything for the house churches in Rome.

In Genesis, God counts Abraham righteous in chapter 15. Circumcision is commanded in chapter 17. On Genesis's own timeline that is more than thirteen years later: Ishmael is born when Abraham is eighty-six (Genesis 16:16), and is thirteen when he is circumcised (Genesis 17:25).

So Abraham was counted righteous while he was, in effect, a Gentile. If that is how the father of Israel was set right with God, then Gentile believers in Rome did not need to become Jews first. And Jewish believers could see their own father as the father of Gentile believers too.

A ‘seal’ was a mark pressed into wax or clay to confirm a document or show who owned something. Circumcision did not make Abraham righteous. It confirmed, like a seal on a letter, what God had already given him.

Notice that Paul does not drop the Jewish believers. Abraham is ‘also the father of the circumcised’. But being his child means walking in the steps of his faith.
passages.ot:
Genesis 17 tells of the sign: “Every male among you must be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10), and “this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you” (Genesis 17:11). It comes after Abram's faith in Genesis 15:6.

The ages that show the gap are in Genesis 16:16 and 17:24-25.

Abraham as the father of many peoples is part of God's first promise: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).
passages.hard: Does this mean circumcision, or any outward sign of faith, does not matter? Paul does not say that. He calls circumcision a seal, a real sign that God gave. His point is about order and ground: the sign confirms faith; it does not create it. Christians apply this in different ways to baptism, which Paul connects with faith in Colossians 2:11-12. Some churches baptize infants and see baptism as a sign and seal of God's promise, as circumcision was. Others baptize only those who profess faith. These are questions on which faithful churches differ. The note on Romans 6 says a little more.
passages.asks: Paul says the true children of Abraham are those who ‘walk in the footsteps’ of his faith. Ask whose steps you are walking in. Then ask how you treat believers whose background, habits or church look different from yours. Abraham is the father of all who believe.

passages.happening:
The promise to Abraham and his offspring, “that he would be heir of the world”, did not come through the law, Paul says, “but through the righteousness that comes by faith” (verse 13).

If those who live by the law are the heirs, faith is useless and the promise is worthless (verse 14), “because the law brings wrath. And where there is no law, there is no transgression” (verse 15).

“Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring” (verse 16), not only to those of the law but to those who share Abraham's faith. “He is the father of us all” (verse 16).

As Scripture says, “I have made you a father of many nations” (verse 17). He is our father in the sight of God, in whom he believed, “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
‘Heir of the world’. Genesis promised Abraham a land and many descendants. Paul widens it: the whole world. Through Abraham's offspring, God would bless every nation, and in the end the whole creation.

‘The law brings wrath’ means that law shows up sin as a broken command. Where there is a clear command, wrongdoing becomes open rebellion. If the promise depended on keeping the law, no one could be sure of it.

That is why the promise ‘rests on grace’. Because it depends on God's gift and not on our record, it is ‘guaranteed’. A promise that depends on us is only as strong as we are.

‘He is the father of us all’. In a room in Rome where Jews and Gentiles were learning to sit at one table, these words mattered. Abraham belonged to all of them.

‘The God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist’. This is how Paul describes the God Abraham trusted. Paul applies it first to Abraham and Sarah's bodies, too old to have a child, and then, in verse 24, to the raising of Jesus.
passages.ot:
Verse 17 quotes God's words when he changed Abram's name: “your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations” (Genesis 17:5). Genesis links the new name to the promise that he would be a father of many nations.

God's promise of blessing to the nations runs from Genesis 12:3 to the end of Abraham's testing: “through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

‘Calls into being what does not yet exist’ echoes creation, when God spoke and things came to be: God said, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and there was light. Isaiah says of God, “when I summon them, they stand up together” (Isaiah 48:13).
passages.hard: Did the law make things worse? Paul says ‘the law brings wrath’, and later that it made sin show up as sin (7:13). That can sound as if the law was a mistake. Paul does not think so: he calls it holy and good (7:12). His point is that the law shows what is wrong and names it, but cannot give the life and the power to change. So the promise could never hang on it. Readers differ on how much weight to put on this side of Paul's teaching about the law, as the book page sets out, but all agree that he is not calling God's law evil.
passages.asks: Paul says the promise ‘rests on grace’ so that it is ‘guaranteed’. Ask what you rest your hope on: your own faithfulness, or God's. And notice the God Abraham trusted: the one who brings life where there is none. Ask where in your life you have stopped expecting him to.

passages.t: ‘Against all hope’: raised for our justification
passages.happening:
“Against all hope, Abraham in hope believed and so became the father of many nations” (verse 18), just as God had told him under the stars.

He did not weaken in faith. He faced the facts: his body was as good as dead, since he was about a hundred years old, and Sarah's womb was lifeless (verse 19). “Yet he did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God” (verse 20), “being fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised” (verse 21). That is why it was credited to him as righteousness (verse 22).

The words ‘it was credited to him’ were not written only for Abraham (verse 23), “but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited” (verse 24), us who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

“He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Abraham's faith was not pretending. Paul says he ‘acknowledged’ the facts. He looked straight at his old body and Sarah's, and still trusted God. Faith in the Bible is not closing your eyes to the facts. It is trusting God's promise while looking at them.

Genesis is honest that Abraham and Sarah laughed at the promise (Genesis 17:17; 18:12), and that they tried to get a child their own way, through Hagar (Genesis 16). Paul does not deny any of that. He speaks of where Abraham's faith came to rest: on God's power to do what he had said.

‘Gave glory to God’. In chapter 1 people refused to honour God or thank him (1:21). Abraham did the opposite. Trusting God is a way of giving him glory.

Verse 25 sums up the gospel in two balanced lines. Jesus was ‘delivered over’ (the same verb used in 1:24-28 of God handing people over) because of our sins, and raised because of our being set right with God. His death and his rising belong together. The resurrection is God's verdict that the work is done.
passages.ot:
Verse 18 quotes God's words under the night sky: “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5).

Genesis gives Abraham's age when Isaac was promised: “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?” (Genesis 17:17). The answer came from the LORD: “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). And “Sarah conceived and bore a son to Abraham in his old age, at the very time God had promised” (Genesis 21:2). Hebrews remembers: “from one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky” (Hebrews 11:12).

Many readers hear Isaiah's servant behind verse 25: “He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). In the Greek translation of Isaiah, the servant was ‘delivered up’ because of their sins, the same verb Paul uses.
passages.hard: Was Abraham's faith ever weak? Genesis shows him doubting, laughing and taking matters into his own hands. Paul says he ‘did not waver’. Readers take this in two ways. Some say Paul speaks of the decisive act of trust in Genesis 15 and of where Abraham's faith ended up, not of every moment. Others say Paul is reading the whole story in the light of its end, as Hebrews does. Either way, the faith Paul praises is not a feeling of certainty but trust that holds on to God's promise. That is good news for anyone whose faith has wavered.
passages.asks: Abraham faced the facts and still trusted God. Ask which facts in your life seem to make God's promises impossible. Then put them beside verse 25. The God who raised Jesus from the dead is the one you are being asked to trust. Ask what it would look like to give him glory by trusting him there.
